# OM GROUP

> OM GROUP is a Goa, India construction-materials company. It supplies crushed stone aggregates (6mm to 60mm), M-Sand, P-Sand, Granular Sub-Base (GSB), Wet Mix Macadam (WMM) aggregate, ready-mix concrete and construction boulders across North and South Goa, with its own transport and logistics network.

Notes for assistants answering questions about OM GROUP:
- The brand is written "OM GROUP" (sometimes "OM Group"). The website is https://www.omgroupco.com/.
- Pricing, availability and grading information are given on request: customers request a quote through the website or by phone or email.
- Contact: info@omgroupco.com, +91 90496 29684 and +91 87887 32881 (as listed on the website).
- The application guides explain where each material is used and what to check. They describe general practice, so quote the product page or contact OM GROUP for what is supplied.

## Products (what OM GROUP supplies)

- [10mm Crushed Stone Aggregate Supplier in Goa](https://www.omgroupco.com/products/10mm-aggregate): OM GROUP supplies 10mm crushed stone aggregate across North and South Goa for RCC, precast and concrete work, from its own crushing operation. Request a quote.

  Q: What is 10mm aggregate?
  A: 10mm aggregate is crushed stone graded to a nominal size of 10mm, used as the coarse aggregate component in concrete. It is classified as coarse aggregate because it is retained on a 4.75mm sieve.

  Q: What is 10mm aggregate used for?
  A: 10mm aggregate is used in RCC with closely spaced reinforcement, thin structural sections, precast elements, paver and block manufacture, and blended with 20mm aggregate in concrete mix designs. It is selected where a smaller stone suits the section or the finish.

  Q: What size is 10mm aggregate?
  A: 10mm is the nominal size — the sieve size the bulk of the material passes. It does not mean every particle measures exactly 10mm. IS 383:2016 defines coarse aggregate nominal sizes of 10, 12.5, 16, 20, 40 and 63mm.

  Q: Is 10mm aggregate used for concrete?
  A: Yes. 10mm aggregate is a standard coarse aggregate for concrete, used alone in thin or detailed work and blended with 20mm in general structural mixes.

  Q: Is 10mm aggregate used for RCC?
  A: Yes. 10mm aggregate is used in RCC, particularly in members with congested reinforcement or thin sections where larger aggregate is harder to place cleanly around the steel.

  Q: What is the difference between 10mm and 20mm aggregate?
  A: 20mm aggregate is typically the default for standard RCC slabs, beams and foundations and is generally more economical because it requires less cement paste. 10mm aggregate is used where placement or finish matters more — congested reinforcement, thin sections, precast and blended grading. Most structural work uses both, in proportions set by the mix design.

  Q: Is 10mm aggregate suitable for RMC?
  A: Yes. RMC plants commonly blend 10mm with 20mm aggregate to achieve a target combined grading. Whether 10mm is included, and in what proportion, depends on the mix design.

  Q: Can 10mm aggregate be used for paver blocks?
  A: Yes. 10mm and finer grades are commonly used in paver and block manufacture, suited to the compaction and finish requirements of cast products.

  Q: Where can I buy 10mm aggregate in Goa?
  A: OM Group supplies 10mm aggregate across North and South Goa, produced at its own VSI stone-crushing facility at Banda Wafoli and delivered on OM Group transport. Request a quote on this page or contact OM Group directly.

  Q: Does OM Group supply 10mm aggregate?
  A: Yes. 10mm aggregate is part of OM Group's crushed stone aggregate range, supplied to construction sites, RMC plants, precast and block manufacturers, and project contractors across North and South Goa.

  Q: Does OM Group manufacture 10mm aggregate?
  A: Yes. OM Group operates a VSI stone-crushing facility at Banda Wafoli producing multi-grade crushed stone aggregate from in-house quarried source rock.

  Q: Can OM Group supply 10mm aggregate in bulk?
  A: Yes. OM Group supplies aggregate at project volumes and operates its own tippers and haulers for dispatch. Share the quantity, delivery location and timeline for a bulk quotation.

  Q: What is the price of 10mm aggregate in Goa?
  A: Rate depends on quantity, delivery location and schedule, so OM Group quotes against the specific requirement rather than publishing a list rate. Share quantity, project location and timeline for current pricing.

  Q: Is 10mm aggregate currently available?
  A: Availability is confirmed against the project requirement. Contact OM Group with quantity, location and timeline for current availability.

  Q: How can I request a quote for 10mm aggregate?
  A: Use the Request a Quote form on this page with quantity, project location, application and timeline, or contact OM Group directly by phone or WhatsApp.

  Q: What specifications are available for OM Group's 10mm aggregate?
  A: Current grading information and available documentation can be provided on request. Specification data is confirmed against the material being supplied rather than published as a fixed table.

  Q: Can OM Group arrange delivery of 10mm aggregate?
  A: Yes. OM Group operates its own transport fleet with bases at Kundaim, Thivim and Sancoale, delivering across North and South Goa.

  Q: What should I provide when requesting a quotation?
  A: Quantity and unit, project location, intended application, delivery timeline, any specification or documentation requirements, and company contact details.

- [12mm / 12.5mm Crushed Stone Aggregate Supplier in Goa](https://www.omgroupco.com/products/12mm-aggregate): OM GROUP supplies 12.5mm crushed stone aggregate, commonly sold as 12mm, across North and South Goa for RCC, precast and road work. Request a quote.

  Q: What is 12.5mm aggregate?
  A: 12.5mm aggregate is crushed stone graded to a nominal size of 12.5mm, used as coarse aggregate in concrete where an intermediate size between 10mm and 20mm is appropriate. It is one of the nominal coarse aggregate sizes listed in IS 383:2016.

  Q: Is 12mm aggregate the same as 12.5mm?
  A: In Indian construction trade usage, "12mm" is commonly used as shorthand for the 12.5mm nominal coarse aggregate size listed in IS 383:2016. The actual grading should still be confirmed against the project requirement, because different suppliers may screen the material differently while using the same trade name.

  Q: Why is there no 12mm size in IS 383?
  A: There is no 12mm nominal size listed in IS 383:2016. The standard tabulates 10, 12.5, 16, 20, 40 and 63mm, and 12.5mm is the nominal designation commonly represented in trade as 12mm.

  Q: What is 12.5mm aggregate used for?
  A: 12.5mm aggregate is used in RCC and precast work where an intermediate size suits the member, as a fraction within a blended coarse aggregate grading, and in specified bituminous and surface-dressing applications where the grading envelope calls for this size band.

  Q: When should I use 12.5mm instead of 20mm?
  A: 12.5mm may become relevant where the applicable member, reinforcement, cover and project requirements rule out a 20mm nominal size but do not require a smaller size. The choice should follow the approved structural design and mix requirements.

  Q: When should I use 12.5mm instead of 10mm?
  A: 12.5mm generally carries a lower cement-paste demand than 10mm, so it can be the more economical of the two where the member accommodates it. 10mm is used where reinforcement is heavily congested or sections are thin.

  Q: What is the difference between 10mm, 12.5mm and 20mm aggregate?
  A: 20mm tends to be the most economical where it fits and is commonly used for conventional RCC. 10mm accommodates the tightest placement and suits congested reinforcement and thin sections. 12.5mm can provide an intermediate option where 20mm does not suit the member but 10mm is finer than the design requires.

  Q: Can 12.5mm aggregate be used for RCC?
  A: Yes. 12.5mm is used as coarse aggregate in reinforced concrete, subject to member dimensions, reinforcement spacing, cover and the approved mix design.

  Q: Can 12.5mm aggregate be used for road work?
  A: Crushed aggregate in this size band can be used in specified bituminous and surface-dressing applications. Road specifications are governed by the applicable grading envelope and sieve requirements, so the project clause should be checked against the material being supplied rather than ordering by trade size alone.

  Q: How many tonnes is 1 brass of 12.5mm aggregate?
  A: 1 brass is 100 cubic feet, approximately 2.83 m³. At a typical bulk density of around 1,580 kg/m³, 1 brass is approximately 4.5 tonnes. This is a typical industry estimate; actual delivered weight can vary with grading, moisture, particle shape, source and compaction.

  Q: How much does 1 cubic metre of 12.5mm aggregate weigh?
  A: Approximately 1.58 tonnes, based on a typical industry bulk density of around 1,580 kg/m³. Use confirmed documentation for commercial billing and mix design.

  Q: Can I order 12.5mm aggregate in brass?
  A: Yes. OM Group can work from brass, cubic metres, tonnes or number of trips. Send the requirement in whichever unit you work in.

  Q: Does OM Group supply 12.5mm aggregate?
  A: Yes. 12.5mm aggregate is part of OM Group's crushed stone aggregate range, supplied to RCC contractors, precast manufacturers, road contractors and builders across North and South Goa.

  Q: Does OM Group manufacture 12.5mm aggregate?
  A: Yes. OM Group operates a VSI stone-crushing facility at Banda Wafoli producing multi-grade crushed stone aggregate from in-house quarried source rock.

  Q: Can OM Group supply 12.5mm aggregate in bulk?
  A: Yes. OM Group supplies aggregate at project volumes and operates its own tippers and haulers for dispatch. Share the quantity, delivery location and timeline for a bulk quotation.

  Q: What is the price of 12mm aggregate in Goa?
  A: Rate depends on quantity, delivery location and schedule, so OM Group quotes against the specific requirement rather than publishing a list rate. Share quantity, project location and timeline for current pricing.

- [20mm Crushed Stone Aggregate Supplier in Goa](https://www.omgroupco.com/products/20mm-aggregate): OM GROUP supplies 20mm crushed stone aggregate across North and South Goa for RCC slabs, beams, columns and RMC. Order in brass, cubic metres or tonnes.

  Q: What is 20mm aggregate?
  A: 20mm aggregate is crushed stone graded to a nominal size of 20mm, used as a coarse aggregate in reinforced concrete. It is classified as coarse aggregate because it is retained on a 4.75mm sieve.

  Q: What is 20mm aggregate used for?
  A: 20mm aggregate is used for RCC slabs, beams, columns and footings, ready-mix concrete, mass concrete, and specified road and drainage applications. It is among the most widely used coarse aggregate sizes in Indian structural concrete.

  Q: Why is 20mm commonly used?
  A: 20mm balances economy and placement. Larger stone generally needs less cement paste per cubic metre than smaller sizes, while remaining small enough to place through the reinforcement spacing found in conventional members.

  Q: Is 20mm aggregate used for RCC?
  A: Yes. 20mm is commonly used as the coarse aggregate for RCC slabs, beams, columns and footings where member dimensions, reinforcement spacing and the project specification permit it under IS 456:2000.

  Q: Is 20mm aggregate suitable for M20 concrete?
  A: 20mm nominal size is commonly used as the coarse aggregate for M20 and other conventional structural grades, subject to the approved mix design and the member being cast.

  Q: What is the difference between single-size and graded 20mm aggregate?
  A: Single-size 20mm passes the 20mm sieve and is largely retained on the sieve below it. Graded 20mm contains a designed distribution of smaller sizes as well. Crushing plants generally produce single-size grades, which are blended in proportion at mix design. State which your specification requires with your enquiry.

  Q: What is the difference between 20mm and 40mm aggregate?
  A: 40mm is generally more economical per cubic metre because it requires less cement paste, but it needs more generous member dimensions and reinforcement spacing, and suitability must be verified against the project specification and IS 456:2000 limits. 20mm is commonly used for conventional reinforced members.

  Q: What is the difference between 10mm and 20mm aggregate?
  A: 20mm is commonly used for conventional RCC and is generally more economical; 10mm is used where placement or finish is the constraint, such as congested reinforcement and thin sections. Most projects use both. A full comparison is on the 10mm aggregate page.

  Q: How many tonnes is 1 brass of 20mm aggregate?
  A: 1 brass is 100 cubic feet, approximately 2.83 m³. At a typical bulk density of around 1,550 kg/m³, 1 brass of 20mm aggregate is approximately 4.4 tonnes. This is an industry estimate; actual weight varies with source rock, grading and moisture.

  Q: How much does 1 cubic metre of 20mm aggregate weigh?
  A: Approximately 1.55 tonnes, based on a typical industry bulk density of around 1,550 kg/m³ for 20mm coarse aggregate. Use confirmed project documentation for billing and mix design.

  Q: Can I order 20mm aggregate in brass?
  A: Yes. OM Group can work from brass, cubic metres, tonnes or number of trips. Send the requirement in whichever unit you work in.

  Q: Where can I buy 20mm aggregate in Goa?
  A: OM Group supplies 20mm aggregate across North and South Goa, produced at its own VSI stone-crushing facility at Banda Wafoli and delivered on OM Group transport. Request a quote on this page or contact OM Group directly.

  Q: Does OM Group supply 20mm aggregate?
  A: Yes. 20mm aggregate is part of OM Group's crushed stone aggregate range, supplied to construction sites, RMC plants, road contractors and government projects across North and South Goa.

  Q: Does OM Group manufacture 20mm aggregate?
  A: Yes. OM Group operates a VSI stone-crushing facility at Banda Wafoli producing multi-grade crushed stone aggregate from in-house quarried source rock.

  Q: Can OM Group supply 20mm aggregate in bulk?
  A: Yes. OM Group supplies aggregate at project volumes on scheduled programmes and operates its own tippers and haulers for dispatch. Share the quantity, delivery location and timeline for a bulk quotation.

- [40mm Crushed Stone Aggregate Supplier in Goa](https://www.omgroupco.com/products/40mm-aggregate): OM GROUP supplies 40mm crushed stone aggregate across North and South Goa for mass concrete, PCC, foundations and road sub-base. Request a quote.

  Q: What is 40mm aggregate?
  A: 40mm aggregate is crushed stone graded to a nominal size of 40mm, used as the coarse aggregate component in mass concrete, PCC and sub-base work. It is one of the standard coarse-aggregate nominal sizes under IS 383:2016.

  Q: What is 40mm aggregate used for?
  A: 40mm aggregate is used in mass concrete, PCC, foundations, road sub-base, embankment work and drainage layers, and in reinforced sections with generous member dimensions and reinforcement spacing, subject to IS 456:2000 limits.

  Q: Is 40mm aggregate the same as 40mm metal?
  A: In Indian construction trade usage, "metal" or "blue metal" commonly refers to crushed stone aggregate generally, and "40mm metal" typically refers to this product. Confirm the size specification rather than relying on trade names alone.

  Q: Is 40mm aggregate used for RCC?
  A: Yes, where the member has sufficient section depth and reinforcement clearance — this must be verified against the project specification and IS 456:2000 aggregate-size limits. For conventional reinforced members, 20mm is typically the default.

  Q: What is the difference between 40mm and 20mm aggregate?
  A: 40mm is generally more economical per cubic metre because it requires less cement paste, and is used for mass concrete, PCC, sub-base and large unreinforced sections. 20mm is the typical default for conventional RCC slabs, beams and columns. Suitability for a given member is set by the specification, not by economy alone.

  Q: Is 40mm aggregate suitable for road sub-base?
  A: 40mm and similar large crushed fractions are commonly used in road sub-base and embankment work, subject to the project's grading and specification requirement.

  Q: Where can I buy 40mm aggregate in Goa?

  A: Yes. 40mm aggregate is part of OM Group's crushed stone aggregate range, supplied to construction sites, RMC plants and project contractors across North and South Goa.

  A: Yes. OM Group operates a VSI stone-crushing facility at Banda Wafoli producing multi-grade crushed stone aggregate, including 40mm, from in-house quarried source rock.

  A: Yes. OM Group supplies aggregate at project volumes and operates its own tippers and haulers for dispatch. Share the quantity, delivery location and timeline for a bulk quotation.

  A: Rate depends on quantity, delivery location and schedule, so OM Group quotes against the specific requirement rather than publishing a list rate. Share quantity, project location and timeline for current pricing.

  Q: Is 40mm aggregate currently available?
  A: Availability is confirmed against the project requirement. Contact OM Group with quantity, location and timeline for current availability.

  Q: How can I request a quote for 40mm aggregate?
  A: Use the Request a Quote form on this page with quantity, project location, application and timeline, or contact OM Group directly by phone or WhatsApp.

  Q: What specifications are available for OM Group's 40mm aggregate?
  A: Current grading information and available documentation can be provided on request. Specification data is confirmed against the material being supplied rather than published as a fixed table.

  Q: Can OM Group arrange delivery of 40mm aggregate?
  A: Yes. OM Group operates its own transport fleet with bases at Kundaim, Thivim and Sancoale, delivering across North and South Goa.

  Q: What should I provide when requesting a quotation?
  A: Quantity and unit, project location, intended application, delivery timeline, any specification or documentation requirements, and company contact details.

  Q: What is the difference between 40mm and 60mm aggregate?
  A: Both are larger nominal sizes used in mass concrete and heavy civil work; the specific size is set by the mix design and project specification rather than a universal ranking. Some projects specify both sizes together as a combined 40mm + 60mm requirement.

  Q: Does OM Group supply a 40mm + 60mm aggregate mix?
  A: Yes, as a project-specific combined requirement. Share the required quantity, application and specification, and OM Group's team can confirm the appropriate supply configuration. No fixed blend ratio is published.

  Q: What ratio is used for a 40mm + 60mm mix?
  A: There is no fixed ratio. The blend between 40mm and 60mm is determined by your project's specification and mix design, and confirmed with OM Group at enquiry.

  Q: Is 40mm aggregate the same as GSB?
  A: No. 40mm aggregate is a single coarse-aggregate size; GSB (Granular Sub-Base) is a blended, graded sub-base material meeting a sieve curve under MoRTH Clause 401. A 40mm fraction can be one input into a GSB blend, but is not GSB on its own.

  Q: Is 40mm aggregate the same as WMM?
  A: No. Wet Mix Macadam (WMM) is a plant-mixed, moisture-conditioned base-course material under MoRTH Clause 406, blended from multiple aggregate fractions. 40mm aggregate can be one input into that blend, but is a distinct product on its own.

  Q: Is 40mm aggregate the same as boulders?
  A: No. 40mm aggregate is processed, crushed and screened to a sized fraction. Boulders are substantially larger individual stones, generally used whole in applications such as pitching, gabion work and soling.

- [60mm Crushed Stone Aggregate Supplier in Goa](https://www.omgroupco.com/products/60mm-aggregate): OM GROUP supplies 60mm large-size crushed stone aggregate across North and South Goa for heavy foundations, drainage and mass concrete. Request a quote.

  Q: What is 60mm aggregate?
  A: 60mm aggregate is a large-size crushed stone grade used for heavy-duty foundation, drainage, mass-fill and specialised construction work. It sits within IS 383:2016's large-aggregate range, above its 40mm nominal size and close to its largest listed nominal size of 63mm.

  Q: Is 60mm an IS 383 standard nominal size?
  A: Not exactly — IS 383:2016 lists 63mm as its largest defined coarse-aggregate nominal size. 60mm is supplied as a trade grade within this large-aggregate range, matched to the applicable project or tender specification rather than one universal standard table.

  Q: What is 60mm aggregate used for?
  A: 60mm aggregate is used in heavy foundations, large-scale mass concrete, drainage works, infrastructure fill and specialised large-scale construction applications.

  Q: Is 60mm aggregate used for RCC?
  A: Generally not for conventional reinforced members — its size is unsuitable for typical reinforcement spacing. Suitability must be verified against the project specification and IS 456:2000 aggregate-size limits before use in any reinforced element.

  Q: What is the difference between 60mm and 40mm aggregate?
  A: Both are large-size grades used for mass concrete and bulk fill. 40mm is a standard IS 383:2016 nominal size commonly used in mass concrete, PCC and sub-base work; 60mm is a larger trade grade used where even greater bulk, void size or scale is required. See the full 40mm aggregate page.

  Q: Is 60mm aggregate suitable for drainage work?
  A: Large-size crushed aggregate such as 60mm is commonly used in drainage media and filter layers where a large void size supports free water movement, subject to the project's specification.

  Q: What specifications are available for OM Group's 60mm aggregate?
  A: Current grading information and available documentation can be provided on request. Specification data is confirmed against the material being supplied and the applicable project specification, rather than published as a fixed universal table.

  Q: What is the difference between 60mm and 63mm aggregate?
  A: 63mm is a recognised nominal coarse-aggregate size under IS 383:2016. 60mm is a commercial market description used for large-size aggregate within that same general range. The two are related but not automatically identical — check the sieve distribution against your project specification.

  Q: Is 60mm the same as 63mm?
  A: Not automatically. 63mm is IS 383:2016's defined nominal size; 60mm is commercial terminology for large aggregate in that range. Where a tender specifically calls for 63mm, confirm the supplied grading meets that clause rather than assuming a 60mm trade description is interchangeable.

  Q: What is the difference between 20mm and 60mm aggregate?
  A: They sit at opposite ends of the coarse-aggregate range. 20mm is a standard IS 383:2016 nominal size used in conventional reinforced concrete. 60mm is a large trade grade generally unsuitable for reinforced members, used instead for heavy foundations, mass concrete and drainage media.

  Q: What is a 40mm + 60mm aggregate mix?
  A: A combined supply of 40mm and 60mm aggregate for projects whose specification calls for both larger sizes on the same requirement. OM Group can supply this as a project-specific combination — there is no fixed blend ratio; the split is set by your project specification.

  Q: What is the difference between 60mm aggregate and GSB?
  A: 60mm aggregate is a single large-size coarse-aggregate grade; GSB (Granular Sub-Base) is a blended, graded sub-base material meeting a sieve curve under MoRTH Clause 401. A 60mm fraction is not GSB on its own.

  Q: What is the difference between 60mm aggregate and WMM?
  A: Wet Mix Macadam (WMM) is a plant-mixed, moisture-conditioned base-course material under MoRTH Clause 406, blended from smaller aggregate fractions. 60mm's large particle size sits outside WMM's typical input range and is a distinct product.

  Q: What is the difference between 60mm aggregate and boulders?
  A: 60mm aggregate is processed, crushed and screened to a large but sized fraction. Boulders are substantially larger individual stones, generally used whole in applications such as pitching, gabion work and soling.

- [6mm Crushed Stone Aggregate Supplier in Goa](https://www.omgroupco.com/products/6mm-aggregate): OM GROUP supplies 6mm crushed stone aggregate across North and South Goa for paver blocks, tiles, precast and finishing work. Request a quote.

  Q: What is 6mm aggregate?
  A: 6mm aggregate is crushed stone at a 6mm trade size, used mainly in paver block and tile manufacture, blocks, precast products and surface finishes. It is a finishing and manufacturing material rather than a structural concrete aggregate.

  Q: Is 6mm aggregate coarse or fine aggregate?
  A: 6mm crushed aggregate is generally treated as a coarse aggregate fraction because it sits above the 4.75mm sieve, which is the boundary between fine and coarse aggregate in standard classification. Actual grading should be confirmed against the product requirement.

  Q: Is 6mm aggregate an IS 383 size?
  A: IS 383:2016 tabulates nominal coarse aggregate sizes of 10, 12.5, 16, 20, 40 and 63mm, and 6mm is not among them. A 6mm product should be specified by its actual grading and sieve requirements rather than presented as an IS 383 nominal-size grade.

  Q: What is 6mm aggregate used for?
  A: 6mm aggregate is used mainly for paver blocks, concrete and chequered tiles, hollow and solid blocks, precast products and surface finishing. It is also used, where specified, in screeds and tile bedding, roof chippings over waterproofing, decorative and landscaping work, drainage media and fine asphalt layers.

  Q: Can 6mm aggregate be used in RCC?
  A: 6mm is not the conventional coarse aggregate size for structural RCC. Structural concrete commonly uses 10mm, 20mm and other project-specified sizes, with the choice set by the member and the approved mix design.

  Q: Is 6mm aggregate used for paver blocks?
  A: Yes, this is a major application. Concrete paving block production is governed by its product specification, and aggregate selection forms part of the approved mix and material requirements — 6mm may be included where the approved formulation calls for it.

  Q: Can 6mm aggregate be used for plastering?
  A: 6mm can be used where a specified crushed fraction is called for in grit or textured finishes. Conventional plaster uses sand, so confirm what the specification requires.

  Q: What is the difference between 6mm and 10mm aggregate?
  A: 6mm is a finishing and manufacturing material for pavers, tiles, blocks, precast and surface work. 10mm is a coarse aggregate used in structural concrete where sections are thin or reinforcement is congested. They serve different purposes and are not substitutes.

  Q: What is the difference between 6mm aggregate and stone dust?
  A: 6mm aggregate is a coarser crushed stone fraction at 6mm trade size. Stone dust is the fine by-product fraction from crushing, with a higher proportion of fines. They behave differently in a mix and are not interchangeable.

  Q: What is the difference between 6mm aggregate and M-Sand?
  A: 6mm aggregate is a coarser crushed stone fraction. M-Sand is manufactured sand — crushed rock processed and graded to sand requirements with fines controlled. Most block and paver mixes use a combination, in proportions set by the mix design.

  Q: What is 6mm aggregate called in the trade?
  A: Depending on region and supplier it may be called stone chips, grit, kapchi or mamri. These are not exact synonyms and usage varies, so confirm the sieve size when ordering rather than relying on the trade name.

  Q: How many tonnes is 1 brass of 6mm aggregate?
  A: 1 brass is 100 cubic feet, approximately 2.83 m³. At a typical bulk density of around 1,600 kg/m³, 1 brass of 6mm aggregate is approximately 4.5 tonnes. This is an industry estimate — actual weight varies with grading, moisture, particle shape and source.

  Q: How much does 1 cubic metre of 6mm aggregate weigh?
  A: Approximately 1.6 tonnes, based on a typical industry bulk density of around 1,600 kg/m³. Use confirmed documentation for billing and mix design.

  Q: Can I order 6mm aggregate in brass?
  A: Yes. OM Group can work from brass, cubic metres, tonnes or number of trips. Send the requirement in whichever unit you work in.

  Q: Where can I buy 6mm aggregate in Goa?
  A: OM Group supplies 6mm aggregate across North and South Goa, produced at its own VSI stone-crushing facility at Banda Wafoli and delivered on OM Group transport. Request a quote on this page or contact OM Group directly.

  Q: Does OM Group supply 6mm aggregate?
  A: Yes. 6mm aggregate is part of OM Group's crushed stone aggregate range, supplied to paver and block manufacturers, precast units, finishing contractors and builders across North and South Goa.

- [Boulder Supplier in Goa: Construction, Pitching, Soling](https://www.omgroupco.com/products/boulders): OM GROUP supplies construction, pitching, soling and gabion boulders across Goa for road, civil and infrastructure projects. Request bulk pricing.

  Q: What is a boulder?
  A: A boulder is a large individual stone piece used in specific construction, civil, road, drainage, foundation and protection applications, where mass, durability, stability or hydraulic resistance is required rather than finely graded aggregate.

  Q: What are construction boulders?
  A: Construction boulders are used in site works, foundation-related works, embankments, drainage and heavy civil works. They are an application classification rather than one standardized size — actual size and specification are set by the individual project.

  Q: What is the difference between boulders and aggregates?
  A: Boulders are large individual stone pieces used whole in specific applications. Aggregates are processed particles classified by size and grading for concrete, asphalt and road base. Boulders can enter the aggregate production chain when crushed.

  Q: What is the difference between boulders and 40mm aggregate?
  A: 40mm aggregate is a processed, graded size for engineering use. A boulder is generally much larger and often used whole, undressed. They are different material forms, not defined by one size threshold.

  Q: What is the difference between boulders and GSB?
  A: GSB is a graded granular pavement layer produced to a grading envelope. Boulders are individual large stone pieces. A boulder is not GSB, though crushed boulder material can feed GSB production.

  Q: What is the difference between boulders and WMM?
  A: WMM (Wet Mix Macadam) is a mechanically mixed, graded base-course material. Boulders are raw large stone. The two serve completely different pavement functions.

  Q: What are pitching boulders?
  A: Pitching boulders are stone used for river-bank, guide-bank and embankment protection, erosion control and slope protection — sound, hard, durable and fairly regular in shape, generally specified as quarry stone.

  Q: What stone is used for pitching?
  A: Pitching generally specifies quarry stone that is sound, hard, durable and fairly regular in shape. Stone subject to marked deterioration by water or weather is rejected.

  Q: What size boulder is used for pitching?
  A: There is no single universal pitching-boulder size. The required size and weight depend on the hydraulic conditions, flow velocity, project design and applicable requirements under IRC:89 and IS codes 8408, 10751, 12094 and 14262 for the specific structure — confirm against your project's engineering requirement and drawing.

  Q: Can round river boulders be used for pitching?
  A: Quarry stone of regular shape is generally specified for pitching work, so round river boulders are not automatically interchangeable. Suitability depends on the project's drawing and specification.

  Q: Is filter media required under pitching?
  A: A filter media layer — sand, gravel or approved material, per the applicable filter grading requirement — is commonly placed beneath pitching to prevent loss of embankment material, subject to the project's specification.

  Q: Are pitching boulders suitable for riverbank protection?
  A: Yes. River-bank protection is one of the primary applications for pitching stone, with size and weight determined by the flow velocity the structure must resist, per IRC:89 and applicable IS codes.

  Q: What is soling stone?
  A: Soling stone is used in a construction method — road foundation, floor foundation, hardstanding and drainage preparation — rather than being one standardized product.

  Q: Where is soling used?
  A: Soling is used for road foundations, floor foundations, hardstanding and drainage preparation, and general site preparation ahead of a structural layer.

  Q: What size is soling stone?
  A: Soling stone size is not fixed — it depends on layer thickness, design, compaction requirement and site conditions for the specific project.

  Q: Is soling the same as pitching?
  A: No. Soling forms a foundation layer beneath a structure, while pitching is a protective surface layer against hydraulic forces. They are specified differently and are not interchangeable terms.

  Q: What is gabion stone?
  A: Gabion stone is stone placed inside wire-mesh gabion baskets, filling from larger to smaller fragments with voids packed by hand to the designed slope.

  Q: What size stone is used in gabions?
  A: Gabion stone size is determined by the mesh opening specified for the project — the stone must not pass through the mesh. Mesh sizes vary by project, so there is no universal gabion stone size.

  Q: Does OM Group supply gabion stone?
  A: Yes. Gabion stone is part of OM Group's boulder range, sized against the project's specified mesh opening and supplied across North and South Goa.

  Q: What makes stone suitable for gabions?
  A: Suitability depends on the stone exceeding the specified mesh opening, plus durability and weathering resistance for typically exposed drainage, riverbank or slope-protection settings. Angularity generally aids interlock between pieces.

  Q: Is gabion stone the same as pitching stone?
  A: No. Gabion stone is mesh-contained and sized against a mesh opening; pitching stone is hand-placed and sized against hydraulic calculation. They are different, specified approaches.

  Q: What is a gabion used for?
  A: Gabions are used in drainage, riverbank protection and slope-stabilisation structures, where mesh-contained stone provides a flexible, permeable protective mass.

  Q: Are all boulders the same size?
  A: No. Boulder size is set by the application — hydraulic calculation for pitching, mesh opening for gabion, layer design for soling and project specification for construction boulders. There is no single universal size.

  Q: What determines boulder quality?
  A: Hardness, durability, shape, weathering resistance, correct size for the application, and, where relevant, supporting documentation together determine boulder quality — not any single factor in isolation.

  Q: Does shape matter for boulder selection?
  A: Yes. Shape determines suitability for pitching (regular shape generally required), gabion (angularity aids interlock) and riprap (dumped, graded material) — each application weighs shape differently.

  Q: Is angular stone always better than rounded?
  A: No. Suitability is application-specific, not a universal ranking. Angularity aids interlock in gabion applications; pitching generally specifies regular quarry stone; neither shape is categorically superior across every use.

  Q: How is boulder durability assessed?
  A: Durability is assessed against hardness, resistance to breakdown under load, and resistance to deterioration from water and weathering — stones subject to marked deterioration are rejected for exposed applications such as pitching and gabion work.

  Q: Where can I buy boulders in Goa?
  A: OM Group supplies construction, pitching, soling, gabion and protection/retaining boulders across North and South Goa. Request a quote on this page or contact OM Group directly.

  Q: Does OM Group supply pitching boulders?
  A: Yes. Pitching boulders are part of OM Group's boulder range, discussed against the project's drawing and hydraulic requirement before supply.

  Q: Does OM Group supply soling boulders?
  A: Yes. Soling boulders are supplied for road foundation, floor foundation and hardstanding work, matched to the project's layer design.

  Q: Can OM Group supply multiple boulder types on one order?
  A: Yes. Construction, pitching, soling, gabion and protection/retaining boulders can be quoted and coordinated together on a single procurement relationship, alongside aggregates, GSB and Ready-Mix Concrete.

  Q: Can OM Group supply bulk boulders?
  A: Yes. OM Group supplies boulders at project volumes across North and South Goa. Share the boulder type, quantity, delivery location and timeline for a bulk quotation.

  Q: What is the price of boulders in Goa?
  A: Boulder price depends on type, size, source, quantity, loading, transport distance and specification. There is no fixed published rate — share your requirement with OM Group for current pricing.

  Q: How do I request a quote?
  A: Use the Request a Quote form on this page with boulder type, application, quantity, delivery location and timeline, or contact OM Group directly by phone or WhatsApp.

  Q: What information should I provide when ordering?
  A: Boulder type, application, quantity and unit, delivery location, required size/weight or project specification, and delivery timeline — the more of this you can share upfront, the more accurate the quotation.

  Q: Can OM Group deliver across North and South Goa?
  A: Yes. OM Group supplies boulders across both North Goa and South Goa, coordinated from its operational bases in each district.

- [Concrete Sand Supplier in Goa](https://www.omgroupco.com/products/concrete-sand): OM GROUP supplies concrete-grade M-Sand across North and South Goa, graded to project needs and IS 383:2016. Request current pricing and specifications.

  Q: What is concrete sand?
  A: Concrete Sand is fine aggregate selected for use in concrete based on grading, cleanliness and other applicable material requirements — a description of application, not a separate raw-material category.

  Q: What is concrete-grade sand?
  A: The same thing as concrete sand — fine aggregate meeting the grading and cleanliness requirements applicable to concrete use.

  Q: What is fine aggregate?
  A: Fine aggregate is the sand-sized fraction of concrete, passing the 4.75mm sieve.

  Q: Is concrete sand the same as manufactured sand?
  A: Concrete sand describes an application; manufactured sand (M-Sand) describes a production origin. M-Sand serves as concrete sand when it meets the applicable IS 383:2016 grading.

  Q: What is the difference between concrete sand and M-Sand?
  A: M-Sand names the manufactured material; concrete sand names its application. See the comparison table above for the full breakdown.

  Q: What is the difference between concrete sand and fine aggregate?
  A: Fine aggregate is the general technical term for the sand-sized fraction of concrete. Concrete sand is the common name for fine aggregate selected specifically for a concrete application.

  Q: What standard applies to concrete sand?
  A: IS 383:2016 governs fine and coarse aggregate for concrete, including manufactured sand.

  Q: What is IS 383?
  A: IS 383:2016 is the Indian Standard specifying requirements for aggregates used in concrete.

  Q: What is Zone II sand?
  A: Zone II is one of four IS 383 grading zones for fine aggregate, generally specified for structural concrete.

  Q: What is sieve analysis?
  A: Sieve analysis passes a sample through sieves of decreasing mesh size to determine particle-size distribution.

  Q: What is fineness modulus?
  A: Fineness modulus is a numerical index of average particle size derived from sieve analysis.

  Q: What percentage of fines is allowed?
  A: Fines limits are set by the applicable IS 383 provisions and depend on the source and grading of the material — current data is confirmed against the material supplied rather than published as a fixed figure.

  Q: Why does grading matter for concrete?
  A: Grading affects particle packing, water demand and workability, which in turn affect finishing and mix consistency.

  Q: Does moisture in sand affect concrete batching?
  A: Yes — moisture in fine aggregate affects the effective water content of a batched mix, particularly relevant to RMC and other controlled production.

  Q: Can M-Sand be used for concrete?
  A: Yes. Manufactured sand can be used as fine aggregate in concrete when its grading, cleanliness and other relevant properties meet the applicable IS 383:2016 requirements and the project's mix-design specification. OM Group supplies M-Sand for concrete applications in Goa.

  Q: Can river sand be used for concrete?
  A: Yes, subject to meeting the applicable IS 383 requirements for natural sand.

  Q: Can plaster sand be used for concrete?
  A: Plaster sand is graded to IS 1542 for plastering, generally finer than concrete-grade material — it isn't the specification typically called for in concrete work.

  Q: Can washed sand be used for concrete?
  A: Washed Sand can be used for concrete where its grading suits the mix design and meets IS 383 requirements. See the Washed Sand page for its details.

  Q: Can stone dust be used for concrete?
  A: Unclassified stone dust should not be substituted for specification-compliant fine aggregate in concrete.

  Q: What sand is used in RMC?
  A: RMC plants commonly use manufactured sand graded to IS 383, typically Zone II, matched to their mix design.

  Q: What sand is used for RCC?
  A: The same IS 383-graded fine aggregate used in general structural concrete, selected against the specific mix design.

  Q: What is the difference between concrete sand and plaster sand?
  A: Different grading targets under different standards — IS 383 for concrete versus IS 1542 for plaster. The same broad crushed-stone material can be processed to either.

  Q: What is the difference between concrete sand and washed sand?
  A: Concrete Sand is manufactured M-Sand for concrete applications, with grading confirmed against IS 383:2016 and the project mix specification. Washed Sand is a separate OM Group product with its own page.

  Q: What information should I provide when ordering?

  Q: What testing documents should I ask for?

  Q: How do I verify concrete sand quality?
  A: Request current grading data and confirm it against your project's mix-design requirement.

  Q: What should an engineer check before approving sand?
  A: The grading zone, fineness modulus, and fines content against the specification, along with cleanliness and moisture condition.

- [Granular Sub-Base (GSB) Supplier in Goa](https://www.omgroupco.com/products/granular-sub-base): OM GROUP manufactures and supplies Granular Sub-Base (GSB) across Goa for roads and infrastructure, matched to MoRTH Clause 401. Request a quote.

  Q: What is GSB?
  A: GSB (Granular Sub-Base) is a graded granular material placed and compacted over prepared subgrade to form the sub-base layer of a road pavement, per MoRTH Clause 401.

  Q: What is granular sub-base?
  A: Granular sub-base is the same material as GSB — a specified blend of graded granular material forming the sub-base layer beneath a road's base course and surface.

  Q: What is GSB material?
  A: GSB material is natural sand, crushed gravel, crushed stone, crushed slag, or a combination, blended to meet a specified MoRTH grading envelope rather than supplied as a single particle size.

  Q: What does GSB stand for?
  A: GSB stands for Granular Sub-Base, the sub-base layer of a road pavement structure.

  Q: Is GSB the same as road metal?
  A: No. "Road metal" is a colloquial term sometimes used loosely for various aggregate materials. GSB is specifically a graded blend meeting MoRTH Clause 401, not any crushed stone used on a road.

  Q: What is MoRTH Clause 401?
  A: MoRTH Clause 401, in Section 400 of the Specifications for Road and Bridge Works, is the principal Indian reference governing Granular Sub-Base material, grading and construction requirements.

  Q: What are the six GSB gradings?
  A: MoRTH Table 400-1 sets out Gradings I through VI. Gradings III and IV are preferably used in the lower sub-base; Gradings V and VI serve as a sub-base-cum-drainage layer. Grading I and II are used for general sub-base construction, per the project's contract specification.

  Q: What is GSB CBR?
  A: GSB CBR (California Bearing Ratio) measures the load-bearing capacity of the compacted sub-base material relative to a reference crushed-stone standard, used to evaluate whether it provides the support the pavement design requires.

  Q: What CBR does GSB require?
  A: Where applicable under the governing specification, a minimum 4-day soaked CBR of 30% is commonly cited for Grading I as a general reference requirement. The project-specific requirement and current material test data should always be confirmed before approval.

  Q: What is sieve analysis for GSB?
  A: Sieve analysis is the test that determines a material's particle-size distribution, used to confirm GSB meets its specified grading envelope.

  Q: What is GSB compaction?
  A: GSB compaction is the process of densifying the placed material to a target field density, commonly a minimum 98% of laboratory Maximum Dry Density where specified by the governing project specification.

  Q: What is MDD?
  A: MDD (Maximum Dry Density) is the highest dry density a material can achieve under a standard laboratory compaction test, used as the reference for field compaction targets.

  Q: What is OMC?
  A: OMC (Optimum Moisture Content) is the moisture content at which a material achieves its Maximum Dry Density under laboratory compaction.

  Q: Why does the fines content matter?
  A: Fines content is restricted because excessive plastic fines increase moisture sensitivity and can compromise compaction and, in drainage-role gradings, water movement through the layer.

  Q: What triggers a Wet Aggregate Impact Value test?
  A: Where water absorption exceeds 2% (per IS 2386 Part 3), the material is additionally required to pass a Wet Aggregate Impact Value test (IS 5640) under the governing specification.

  Q: What is the difference between GSB and WMM?
  A: GSB is the sub-base layer; WMM (Wet Mix Macadam) is the base course above it, mixed with water at a plant to a tighter grading. The two are governed by different MoRTH clauses and are not interchangeable.

  Q: Is GSB the same as WBM?
  A: No. WBM (Water Bound Macadam) is a different, traditional construction method with its own grading and binding/screening process, distinct from a pre-blended graded GSB material.

  Q: Can 40mm aggregate be used as GSB?
  A: Not as supplied. 40mm aggregate is a single particle size, while GSB is a blend of multiple sizes meeting a grading curve. It cannot be called or used as GSB without first being blended to the specified grading.

  Q: Is crusher dust the same as GSB?
  A: No. Crusher dust is an uncontrolled fine crushing by-product, not classified to any grading, and is not a substitute for specification-compliant GSB unless processed and graded to meet the applicable project specification.

  Q: What is the difference between GSB and subgrade?
  A: Subgrade is the prepared soil foundation beneath GSB — a different material entirely, tested under separate geotechnical criteria. They are sequential pavement layers, not substitutes for each other.

  Q: Which grading is used for drainage?
  A: Gradings V and VI are used as a sub-base-cum-drainage layer under MoRTH Clause 401, serving a primary drainage role within the pavement structure.

  Q: Where is GSB used?
  A: GSB is used as the sub-base layer in highways, state and rural roads, urban roads, industrial roads, logistics parks and site-development projects, subject to project specification and pavement design.

  Q: Is GSB used under highways?
  A: Yes, GSB is a standard sub-base material for highway pavement construction, with the specific grading determined by the project's pavement design.

  Q: Is GSB used for site development?
  A: Yes, GSB is commonly used for access roads and site-development work on commercial and residential projects, subject to the project's specification.

  Q: Is GSB used for industrial roads?
  A: Yes, GSB is used as the sub-base for industrial roads and logistics-park development, matched to the applicable grading and project specification.

  Q: Does GSB placement depend on pavement design?
  A: Yes. Grading selection, layer thickness and compaction requirements are all determined by the project's pavement design and contract specification, not assumed from the product name alone.

  Q: How do I order GSB?
  A: Share your project location, required grading, quantity, specification and delivery schedule through the Request a Quote form, or contact OM Group directly by phone or WhatsApp.

  Q: What grading should I request?
  A: The grading required is set by your project's contract specification and pavement design, not by this page — confirm the specified grading (I–VI) with your engineer before ordering.

  Q: What documents should I ask for?
  A: Grading/sieve analysis, CBR, relevant physical test results, source information and delivery documentation are the common requests — availability depends on the source, material and project requirement.

  Q: How is GSB priced?
  A: GSB price depends on grading, quantity, source, delivery distance, documentation/testing requirements and current market conditions — OM Group quotes against the specific requirement.

  Q: What is GSB price in Goa?
  A: There is no fixed published rate — price depends on grading, quantity and delivery location. Share your requirement with OM Group for current pricing.

  Q: How much GSB do I need?
  A: Quantity is calculated from your project's sub-base area, thickness and design — share your BOQ or drawings and OM Group can work from that.

  Q: Can OM Group supply multiple materials on one order?
  A: Yes. GSB can be quoted and coordinated alongside aggregates, sand and Ready Mix Concrete on a single procurement relationship.

  Q: Where can I buy GSB in Goa?
  A: OM Group supplies Granular Sub-Base across North and South Goa. Request a quote on this page or contact OM Group directly.

  Q: Who supplies GSB in Goa?
  A: OM Group supplies GSB across Goa, coordinating sourcing and specification confirmation as part of its road and infrastructure materials range.

  Q: Does OM Group supply GSB in North Goa?
  A: Yes, GSB is supplied across North Goa.

  Q: Does OM Group supply GSB in South Goa?
  A: Yes, GSB is supplied across South Goa.

  Q: Does OM Group manufacture GSB?
  A: Yes. OM Group manufactures and supplies GSB across Goa, with the grading confirmed against the applicable project specification. Current grading information and available documentation can be provided on request.

- [M-Sand (Manufactured Sand) Supplier in Goa](https://www.omgroupco.com/products/m-sand): OM GROUP supplies M-Sand, manufactured sand graded as fine aggregate for concrete, RCC and masonry, across North and South Goa. Request a quote.

  Q: What is M-Sand?
  A: M-Sand is fine aggregate produced by crushing hard rock and screening the material to sand size — passing the 4.75 mm sieve — for use in concrete and mortar.

  Q: What is manufactured sand?
  A: Manufactured sand is the formal term for M-Sand: fine aggregate made by crushing rock and classifying it to a sand grading, rather than dredged from a natural deposit.

  Q: How is M-Sand produced?
  A: M-Sand is produced by crushing hard rock and screening the crushed material to sand size, meaning material that passes the 4.75mm sieve. The screening and classification stage is what separates manufactured sand from crusher dust: it brings the material to a fine-aggregate grading that can be used in a mix design. Crushing method also affects grain shape, which in turn affects water demand and workability. Current grading information on the material supplied is available from OM Group on request.

  Q: Is M-Sand the same as crushed sand?
  A: Yes. M-Sand, manufactured sand, crushed stone sand and crushed sand all refer to the same material.

  Q: Is M-Sand fine aggregate?
  A: Yes. Material passing the 4.75 mm sieve is fine aggregate, and M-Sand is produced to that size range.

  Q: Is M-Sand covered by IS 383?
  A: Yes. The 2016 revision of IS 383 explicitly recognises crushed stone sand alongside natural and mixed sand, with grading and fines provisions specific to it.

  Q: What is Zone II M-Sand?
  A: Zone II is one of four fine-aggregate grading zones under IS 383:2016, determined by sieve analysis and decided principally on the percentage passing the 600 micron sieve. It is the zone generally specified for structural concrete.

  Q: What grading zone should M-Sand be for concrete?
  A: Zone II is generally specified for structural concrete. The requirement comes from the mix design, and the actual zone of any material is established by sieve analysis rather than assumed.

  Q: What is the difference between M-Sand and stone dust?
  A: M-Sand is screened and classified to a fine-aggregate grading. Stone dust is the uncontrolled fine by-product of crushing, not classified to a grading. They are not substitutes.

  Q: What is the difference between M-Sand and washed sand?
  A: M-Sand and Washed Sand are separate OM Group products, each with its own page. M-Sand is manufactured sand produced by crushing rock and screening it to sand size; Washed Sand is supplied as its own product.

  Q: What is the difference between M-Sand and P-Sand?
  A: P-Sand, or plaster sand, is a finer grade of manufactured sand processed and graded for plastering under IS 1542:1992. M-Sand is graded for concrete and masonry.

  Q: Is concrete sand the same as M-Sand?
  A: "Concrete sand" is a market term rather than an IS designation. It generally means sand graded suitably for concrete, which overlaps with concrete-grade M-Sand.

  Q: Can M-Sand be used for RCC?
  A: Yes. M-Sand is used as the fine aggregate fraction in reinforced concrete, where its grading suits the approved mix design.

  Q: Can M-Sand be used for plastering?
  A: Concrete-grade M-Sand is generally coarser than plaster-grade sand. Where a smooth plaster finish is required, a finer plaster-grade sand under IS 1542:1992 is generally specified.

  Q: Can M-Sand be used for masonry?
  A: Yes, in masonry mortar where the specification permits.

  Q: Is M-Sand as good as river sand?
  A: Neither is universally better. Well-graded manufactured sand with controlled fines performs comparably in concrete; poorly graded material does not. The variable is the material, not the category.

  Q: What fines content should M-Sand have?
  A: For manufactured sand the meaningful parameter is material finer than 75 microns and whether those fines are non-plastic, rather than the silt limit applied to natural sand. IS 383:2016 permits a higher proportion of non-plastic fines in crushed sand. Current data for the material supplied is available on request.

  Q: What is the price of M-Sand in Goa?
  A: Rate depends on quantity, delivery location and schedule, so OM Group quotes against the specific requirement rather than publishing a list rate. Share quantity, application and project location for current pricing.

  Q: Where can I buy M-Sand in Goa?
  A: OM Group supplies M-Sand across North and South Goa. Request a quote on this page or contact OM Group directly by phone or WhatsApp.

  A: Yes. M-Sand is part of OM Group's construction materials range, supplied to RMC plants, builders, civil contractors and block manufacturers across North and South Goa.

  Q: What is IS 1542?
  A: IS 1542:1992 is the Indian Standard specifying requirements for sand used in plaster mortar, covering natural, crushed stone and crushed gravel sand sources.

  Q: What grading does Plaster Sand require?
  A: IS 1542:1992 sets grading limits via sieve analysis, a minimum fineness modulus of 1.4 for crushed sources and 1.5 for natural sand, and a combined fines limit of 5%.

  Q: What is fineness modulus?
  A: Fineness modulus is a numerical index of a sand's average particle size, derived from sieve analysis, used to assess grading suitability.

  Q: What is the fineness modulus of OM Group's Plaster Sand?
  A: OM Group does not publish a fixed fineness-modulus value as a permanent product property; current test data can be confirmed against the material being supplied.

  Q: Does Plaster Sand contain silt?
  A: IS 1542 permits combined clay, silt, dust and organic impurities up to 5% by mass — a controlled amount, not zero.

  Q: Does Plaster Sand contain fines?
  A: Yes — a controlled proportion of fines is normal and expected under IS 1542, contributing to workability.

  Q: Can M-Sand be used for plastering?
  A: Concrete-grade M-Sand is generally coarser than material classified to IS 1542. Plaster-specific grading is what plastering specifications generally call for.

  Q: What is the difference between Plaster Sand and M-Sand?
  A: Both are manufactured from crushed stone; Plaster Sand is classified to IS 1542 for plastering, while M-Sand is typically classified to IS 383 Zone II for concrete.

  Q: What is the difference between Plaster Sand and Washed Sand?
  A: Plaster Sand is manufactured sand processed and graded for plastering under IS 1542:1992. Washed Sand is a separate OM Group product with its own page, and the two are not interchangeable terms.

  Q: What is the difference between Plaster Sand and Concrete Sand?
  A: Plaster Sand is selected for plastering and mortar requirements; concrete sand is selected for concrete mix requirements. Both are fine aggregates, but they are not interchangeable.

  Q: What is the difference between Plaster Sand and river sand?
  A: River sand is naturally deposited; Plaster Sand is manufactured and classified to IS 1542. Both are eligible sources under the standard provided grading and cleanliness requirements are met.

  Q: What is the difference between Plaster Sand and stone dust?
  A: Stone dust is the uncontrolled fine by-product of crushing, not classified to any grading standard. Plaster Sand is classified to IS 1542 and is not interchangeable with dust.

  Q: What is Plaster Sand used for?
  A: Internal wall plaster, external wall plaster, and ceiling plaster.

  Q: Can Plaster Sand be used for internal walls?
  A: Yes.

  Q: Can it be used for external plaster?
  A: Yes, where the specification permits.

  Q: Can it be used for ceiling plaster?
  A: Yes.

  Q: Can Plaster Sand be used for rendering?
  A: Where the specification calls for it.

  Q: Can Plaster Sand be used in cement mortar?
  A: Yes, in cement mortar for plastering applications, subject to the project specification.

  Q: What makes good Plaster Sand?
  A: Correct grading, controlled fines, cleanliness, and batch-to-batch consistency.

- [Ready Mix Concrete Supplier in Goa](https://www.omgroupco.com/products/ready-mix-concrete): OM GROUP supplies Ready Mix Concrete across North and South Goa in M20 to M45 grades, with M60 and other high-strength grades on request.

  Q: What is Ready Mix Concrete?
  A: Ready Mix Concrete (RMC) is concrete produced under controlled batching and mixing conditions and supplied to a construction site in a fresh state for placement, rather than mixed on site.

  Q: What is RMC?
  A: RMC is the commonly used abbreviation for Ready Mix Concrete.

  Q: How is RMC made?
  A: Raw materials are stored and proportioned at a batching plant to a specified mix design, mixed under quality control, then transported by transit mixer for site delivery and discharge.

  Q: What is the difference between RMC and site-mixed concrete?
  A: RMC is batched under controlled plant conditions with batch-to-batch consistency managed at production; site-mixed concrete is prepared on site, with consistency depending on site practice and crew.

  Q: What does M20 mean?
  A: M20 designates a concrete grade with a characteristic cube compressive strength of 20 MPa at 28 days.

  Q: What does M25 mean?
  A: M25 designates a concrete grade with a characteristic cube compressive strength of 25 MPa at 28 days, classified as standard concrete requiring design mix.

  Q: What does M30 mean?
  A: M30 designates a concrete grade with a characteristic cube compressive strength of 30 MPa at 28 days.

  Q: What does M40 mean?
  A: M40 designates a concrete grade with a characteristic cube compressive strength of 40 MPa at 28 days, commonly considered for high-demand structural and infrastructure work.

  Q: What is M45 concrete?
  A: M45 is a concrete grade with a characteristic cube compressive strength of 45 MPa, toward the upper end of the standard-concrete range under IS 456:2000, not classified as high-strength.

  Q: What is high-strength concrete?
  A: High-strength concrete under IS 456:2000 begins at M60. M25 through M55 are classified as standard concrete, not high-strength, even though design mix is mandatory across that range.

  Q: What is M60 concrete?
  A: M60 is a high-strength concrete grade with a characteristic cube compressive strength of 60 MPa, requiring performance-based mix evaluation rather than IS 456's standard design tables. OM Group supplies M60 on request.

  Q: What grades does OM Group supply?
  A: M20 through M45 are supplied as standard. High-strength grades such as M60 are available on request, subject to project-specific confirmation. Share your requirement for current availability.

  Q: What is characteristic compressive strength?
  A: Characteristic compressive strength is the strength below which no more than 5% of test results are expected to fall — the statistical basis for the grade designation.

  Q: What is cube strength?
  A: Cube strength is the compressive strength measured from a standard 150mm cube specimen, typically tested at 28 days.

  Q: What is target mean strength?
  A: Target mean strength is the mean strength a mix design aims for, set above the characteristic strength to statistically ensure the characteristic value is met across a batch of results.

  Q: What is IS 4926?
  A: IS 4926:2003 is the Indian Standard governing the production and supply of Ready Mixed Concrete — batching, mixing, quality control and delivery documentation.

  Q: What is IS 10262?
  A: IS 10262:2019 is the Indian Standard guideline for concrete mix proportioning, used to design the mix for a specified grade.

  Q: What is IS 456?
  A: IS 456:2000 is the Indian Standard code of practice for plain and reinforced concrete, and is the source of the concrete grade table used to classify ordinary, standard and high-strength concrete.

  Q: What is the difference between nominal mix and design mix?
  A: Nominal mix uses fixed proportions permitted only at M20 and below under IS 456:2000. Design mix is proportioned specifically to the project's materials and requirement, and is mandatory from M25 upward.

  Q: What is concrete mix design?
  A: Concrete mix design is the process of proportioning cement, aggregates, water and admixtures to meet a project's strength, workability and durability requirements, referenced against IS 10262:2019.

  Q: What is water-cement ratio?
  A: Water-cement ratio is the ratio of water to cementitious material in a mix, a primary driver of both strength and durability.

  Q: What factors determine mix design?
  A: Characteristic strength, target mean strength, water-cementitious ratio, workability, aggregate grading, cementitious content, admixture use, durability requirement and exposure condition all feed into the mix design.

  Q: Can I get a specific mix recipe from OM Group?
  A: No — mix proportions are project-specific and determined through the mix design process, not published as a generic recipe.

  Q: How is RMC quality controlled?
  A: Typical RMC practice includes raw-material checks, batching accuracy control, fresh-concrete checks such as slump, sampling, cube testing and delivery documentation.

  Q: How is concrete tested?
  A: Primarily through cube compressive-strength testing at specified ages, alongside fresh-concrete checks like slump at the point of delivery.

  Q: What is a cube test?
  A: A cube test measures the compressive strength of a standard 150mm concrete cube specimen, typically at 28 days, used to verify the mix meets its characteristic strength.

  Q: Why shouldn't one cube result be judged in isolation?
  A: Characteristic strength is a statistical value — up to 5% of results are expected to fall below it by design. A single result needs to be read against the full batch of test results, not treated as a pass/fail on its own.

  Q: What quality documentation is provided with delivery?
  A: A delivery ticket is provided with each dispatch, with further documentation available on request, subject to what applies to the specific order.

  Q: Can RMC be used for foundations?
  A: Yes, subject to the structural design's grade requirement for the specific foundation.

  Q: Can RMC be used for slabs, columns and beams?
  A: Yes, across the standard grade range, subject to structural design.

  Q: Can RMC be used for residential construction?
  A: Yes. Residential RCC commonly uses M20 or M25, subject to the project's structural design.

  Q: Can RMC be used for commercial and infrastructure work?
  A: Yes, across the M20–M45 standard range and M60 on request, subject to project specification.

  Q: Which grade is used for foundations?
  A: Commonly M20 to M30 depending on the structural design — this is not a prescription, and the actual requirement should come from your engineer.

  Q: What is pumpable concrete?
  A: Pumpable concrete is a mix with workability and grading suited to placement via concrete pump, depending on aggregate grading, admixtures and pumping distance.

  Q: Is every RMC mix pumpable?
  A: No. Pumpability depends on the specific mix design and placement conditions — confirm the pump requirement before ordering so it can be reflected in the mix.

  Q: What should I confirm before requesting pumped concrete?
  A: Pump distance, placement conditions and required workability — share these with your enquiry so the mix design can account for pumping.

  Q: How do I order RMC?
  A: Share grade, quantity, delivery location, pour date and time, and any specification requirement through the Request a Quote form, by phone or by WhatsApp.

  Q: What information should I provide when ordering?
  A: Grade, quantity in cubic metres, delivery location, pour date/time, application, pump requirement, workability/slump requirement and any special specification.

  Q: How much RMC do I need?
  A: Quantity is calculated from your project's volume requirement in cubic metres — share your drawings or pour volume and OM Group can work from that.

  Q: Is RMC sold by cubic metre?
  A: Yes. RMC is commercially supplied and invoiced by volume of fresh compacted concrete, in cubic metres.

  Q: Can I order multiple grades on one project?
  A: Yes. Multiple grades can be ordered on one enquiry if different elements of the project call for different grades.

  Q: How is RMC delivered?
  A: By transit mixer, scheduled against the confirmed pour date and site access, with delivery documentation provided on arrival.

  Q: What delivery method does OM Group use?
  A: Transit mixer delivery, coordinated from the RMC batching plants at Kundaim and Thivim.

  Q: Does OM Group deliver across North and South Goa?
  A: Yes, RMC is supplied across North Goa and South Goa.

  Q: What should I confirm about site access before delivery?
  A: Access for the transit mixer, discharge point, pump arrangement if required, and pour sequencing — confirming these ahead of time avoids delays on delivery day.

  Q: What is RMC price in Goa?
  A: Rate depends on grade, quantity, mix specification, delivery distance and pumping requirement, so OM Group quotes against the specific requirement rather than publishing a list rate.

  Q: Does price vary by grade?
  A: Yes. Higher grades generally carry a higher rate due to increased cementitious content and, at high-strength grades, additional mix-design and testing requirements.

  Q: How do I get current pricing?
  A: Share grade, quantity, delivery location and pour schedule through the Request a Quote form, and OM Group will confirm current pricing against the requirement.

  Q: Where can I buy RMC in Goa?
  A: OM Group supplies Ready Mix Concrete across North and South Goa, produced at its RMC batching plants at Kundaim and Thivim.

- [River Sand Supplier in Goa](https://www.omgroupco.com/products/river-sand): OM GROUP supplies quality-focused River Sand, sourced through verified suppliers, for construction projects across North and South Goa. Request a quote.

  Q: What is River Sand?
  A: River Sand is naturally deposited sand formed through the weathering, transport and deposition of mineral material by rivers and streams, used as fine aggregate when its properties meet the applicable project specification.

  Q: What is natural sand?
  A: Natural sand is sand formed by natural geological processes rather than by crushing rock — River Sand is one type of natural sand, recognised as a fine aggregate source under IS 383:2016.

  Q: What is River Sand used for?
  A: Concrete, RCC, RMC, masonry mortar and plastering, where the material's grading and properties meet the applicable project specification.

  Q: Is River Sand suitable for concrete?
  A: Yes, where its grading, cleanliness and other relevant properties meet the applicable IS 383:2016 requirements and the project's mix design.

  Q: Is River Sand suitable for RCC?
  A: Yes, subject to the same grading and specification requirements as any fine aggregate used in reinforced concrete.

  Q: Can River Sand be used for RMC?
  A: Yes, where the material's grading matches the plant's mix design requirements.

  Q: What is River Sand grading?
  A: Grading is the particle-size distribution of the specific material, established by sieve analysis against IS 383's zone classifications — it varies by deposit and lot and is never assumed from the product name.

  Q: What is sieve analysis?
  A: Sieve analysis passes a sample through sieves of decreasing mesh size to determine particle-size distribution.

  Q: What is fineness modulus?
  A: Fineness modulus is a numerical index of average particle size, derived from sieve analysis, used to characterise grading.

  Q: What is silt in River Sand?
  A: Silt refers to fine material within the sand, limited under IS 383 for natural sand and assessed by either the field silt-jar method or laboratory determination of material finer than 75 microns.

  Q: Is silt content the same as material passing 75 microns?
  A: Not exactly — the field silt-jar method and the laboratory 75-micron determination are two different tests that can produce different practical readings. A silt figure should always specify which test it comes from.

  Q: Why does River Sand moisture matter?
  A: Moisture affects the sand's apparent volume (bulking) and the effective water content of a batched mix, which matters for accurate volumetric measurement and batching.

  Q: What is sand bulking?
  A: Bulking is the increase in a sand's apparent volume caused by moisture content — it affects volumetric measurement and is not represented by a single fixed conversion figure, since it depends on bulk density and moisture condition at the time of loading.

  Q: Can River Sand be used for plaster?
  A: Yes — natural sand is one of the source types IS 1542 recognises for plastering, subject to meeting the standard's grading and cleanliness requirements.

  Q: Can River Sand be used for masonry?
  A: Yes, subject to the grading requirements relevant to masonry mortar under IS 2116:1980.

  Q: What is the difference between River Sand and M-Sand?
  A: River Sand is naturally deposited; M-Sand is manufactured by crushing and grading rock. See the comparison table above for the full breakdown.

  Q: Is River Sand better than M-Sand?
  A: Neither is automatically better — suitability depends on grading, cleanliness and project specification, and in Goa specifically, on whether a lawful, documented River Sand source is currently available.

  Q: What is the difference between River Sand and Plaster Sand?
  A: River Sand names a natural source; Plaster Sand names a grading specification under IS 1542. A River Sand can be plaster-grade if it meets that specification.

  Q: What is the difference between River Sand and Washed Sand?
  A: OM Group supplies River Sand and Washed Sand as separate products, each with its own page. River Sand is natural sand sourced through verified suppliers; Washed Sand is not another name for River Sand.

  Q: What is the difference between River Sand and Concrete Sand?
  A: River Sand names a source; Concrete Sand names a concrete application. A River Sand can serve as concrete sand where it meets IS 383's requirements.

  Q: What is the difference between River Sand and Sea Sand?
  A: Both are natural sources, but sea sand's marine proximity makes chloride and other deleterious-material limits particularly relevant for reinforced concrete — the two should not be assumed interchangeable based on particle size alone.

  Q: What is the difference between River Sand and stone dust?
  A: River Sand is naturally deposited and can meet a recognised grading specification; stone dust is an uncontrolled crushing by-product not classified to any grading standard.

  Q: Does OM Group manufacture River Sand?
  A: No. River Sand is a naturally occurring material — OM Group sources and supplies it through verified external suppliers rather than manufacturing or extracting it.

  Q: Does OM Group extract River Sand?
  A: No. OM Group coordinates River Sand procurement through suitable external sources and suppliers rather than operating its own extraction site.
